```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(knitr.kable.NA = "")
# All numbers in this article come from the CSV files in benchmark-data/,
# written by the benchmark scripts (see "Reproducing the benchmark").
d <- function(f) read.csv(file.path("benchmark-data", f))
tot <- d("totals_biscay.csv")
sc  <- d("xmhw_scaling_block.csv")
agr <- d("agreement_block.csv")
cmp <- jsonlite::read_json(file.path("benchmark-data", "compare_xmhw.json"))
row <- function(cfg) tot[tot$configuration == cfg, ]
s   <- function(cfg) row(cfg)$total_s
blk <- function(v, n) sc$total[sc$variant == v & sc$threads == n]
ratio <- function(a, b) formatC(a / b, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")
secs <- function(x) if (x < 100) sprintf("%.1f s", x) else sprintf("%.1f min", x / 60)
bsec <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f s", x)  # block timings, in seconds
hw8  <- "heatwave3, 8 threads"
hw1  <- "heatwave3, 1 thread"
x1   <- "xmhw, 1 core"
xp8  <- "xmhw, dask processes, 8 workers"
xd8  <- "xmhw, dask distributed, 8 workers"
xt8  <- "xmhw, 8 independent processes on tiles"
hwr  <- "heatwaveR, 1 core (projected from 20 × 20)"
mhw  <- "marineHeatWaves, 1 core (projected from 20 × 20)"
```

## Overview

Marine heatwave (MHW) detection on a gridded product repeats the same
per-pixel calculation, namely a climatology and a threshold, then event
detection, for every ocean pixel. How long this takes decides whether a
regional analysis is run once and stored, or re-run whenever a setting
changes. Here we compare the wall-clock time and memory of four packages that
implement the Hobday et al. (2016, 2018) definition, on the same file and the
same machine, and check that they detect the same events:

1. **heatwave3**, C++ with `std::thread` over pixels and direct NetCDF input
   and output;
2. **heatwaveR**, the R package heatwave3 is ported from, one pixel at a
   time;
3. **marineHeatWaves** (Python), the original implementation of the
   definition, one pixel at a time;
4. **xmhw** (Python), built on xarray and dask, which can run in parallel.

Because xmhw is the only other package designed to run in parallel, most of
the work below is spent finding the fastest way to run it on the 8 cores of
the test machine.

## Data and settings

The input is the Copernicus Marine GLORYS12 reanalysis
(`cmems_mod_glo_phy_my_0.083deg_P1D-m`, dataset version 202311,
[doi:10.48670/moi-00021](https://doi.org/10.48670/moi-00021)), sea water
potential temperature (`thetao`, °C) at the surface level (0.494 m), for the
Bay of Biscay (10°W to 1°W, 43°N to 48°N). The grid is 61 × 109 pixels at
1/12°, of which 5,569 are ocean, with 12,053 daily values from 1993-01-01 to
2025-12-31. heatwave3 and xmhw read the same float32 NetCDF-4 file, and
heatwaveR and marineHeatWaves read the same values for their 20 × 20 block
(see below) from a CSV file.

```{r study-area, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%", fig.alt = "Map of the Bay of Biscay study area, coloured by the mean sea surface temperature from 1993 to 2025, between 14 and 17 °C."}
knitr::include_graphics("benchmark-data/map_study_area_mean_sst.png")
```

All packages use the same settings: a climatology over 1993 to 2022, the 90th
percentile threshold, an 11-day window (half-width 5 days), 31-day smoothing
of the climatology and threshold, a minimum duration of 5 days, gaps of up to
2 days joined, and the Hobday et al. (2018) categories.

| Package | Version | Language and parallelism |
|---------|---------|--------------------------|
| heatwave3 | 1.4.1 (GitHub, commit `4691135`) | C++ core, `std::thread` over pixels |
| heatwaveR | 1.0.0 (GitHub, commit `e0ae30d`) | R + C++, one pixel at a time |
| marineHeatWaves | 0.28 (GitHub, commit `d7292bf`) | Python, one pixel at a time |
| xmhw | 1.0.0 (GitHub tag) | Python, xarray + dask |

heatwave3 was timed through its Python package, which calls the same C++ core
as the R package. The machine is an Apple M2 (4 performance and 4 efficiency
cores, 16 GB RAM) running macOS, with Python 3.12 and R 4.6.1.

## Timing protocol

Each timed run is a fresh process, so no cache, thread pool or memory carries
over between runs, and package imports are not timed.

- **heatwave3** and **xmhw** run on the whole zone, and the time includes
  reading the input file, computing the climatology, detecting the events and
  writing all outputs to NetCDF. heatwave3 is the median of 3 runs after a
  discarded warm-up run. xmhw on the whole zone is a single run per
  configuration (the serial run takes `r secs(s(x1))`).
- **heatwaveR** and **marineHeatWaves** process one pixel at a time and are
  too slow to run on the whole zone. Each runs on a 20 × 20 block of ocean
  pixels with the data already in memory (computation only, which favours
  them), and the time is projected to the whole zone as
  block time / 400 × 5,569. The cost per ocean pixel is constant here, since
  every ocean pixel has the full series. The fastest of 3 runs is used.
- Peak memory is the peak resident set size of the run, summed over all
  processes where a run uses several (xmhw with dask workers or on tiles).

## Results

```{r totals-fig, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%", fig.alt = "Horizontal bar chart on a log scale of the time for climatology plus detection on the whole Bay of Biscay zone, for heatwaveR, marineHeatWaves, four xmhw configurations and heatwave3 on 1 and 8 threads."}
knitr::include_graphics("benchmark-data/totals_biscay.png")
```

```{r totals-table, echo = FALSE}
tt <- tot[, c("configuration", "climatology_s", "detection_s", "total_s",
              "peak_ram_gb", "x_heatwave3_8_threads", "timed")]
tt$x_heatwave3_8_threads <- round(tt$x_heatwave3_8_threads)
knitr::kable(tt, digits = 1, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
             col.names = c("Configuration", "Climatology (s)", "Detection (s)",
                           "Total (s)", "Peak RAM (GB)",
                           "× heatwave3 (8 threads)", "Timed"))
```

heatwave3 processes the whole zone in `r secs(s(hw8))` on 8 threads and in
`r secs(s(hw1))` on one. On a single core it is
`r ratio(s(hwr), s(hw1))` times faster than heatwaveR and
`r ratio(s(x1), s(hw1))` times faster than xmhw, even though the heatwaveR
projection leaves out reading the file. The fastest xmhw configuration on 8
cores takes `r secs(min(s(xp8), s(xd8), s(xt8)))`, i.e.
`r ratio(min(s(xp8), s(xd8), s(xt8)), s(hw8))` times as long as heatwave3 on
8 threads.

## xmhw on 8 cores

### How xmhw runs in parallel

xmhw parallelises over grid cells, not over chunks of the input array. Its
`threshold()` stacks the ocean cells and builds one small dask computation per
cell, and `detect()` builds one `dask.delayed` task per cell. Each function
then runs a single `dask.compute()` over all cells. Two consequences follow.
First, chunking the input `DataArray` adds no parallelism, and it makes every
per-cell task read from the file lazily, so the input should be loaded into
memory first. Second, the number of cells processed at once is set by the
dask *scheduler*, and with no scheduler configured dask uses its threaded
scheduler on all cores, so an xmhw run without explicit settings is already
multi-threaded.

It is important to note one step that is easy to miss. `threshold()` returns
its climatology as lazy dask arrays that carry the computations of every
cell. Passed to `detect()` unchanged, they are sliced per cell, and the time
dask spends optimising the resulting task graph grows with the square of the
number of cells: on 400 cells, detection took 0.72 s per cell this way and
ca. 0.02 s per cell once the climatology was loaded with `.load()`. Every xmhw
timing in this article loads the climatology before `detect()`, as below.

```python
import dask
import xarray as xr
from xmhw.xmhw import threshold, detect

sst = xr.open_dataset("biscay_glorys12_full_1993-2025.nc")["thetao"].load()
with dask.config.set(scheduler="processes", num_workers=8):
    clim = threshold(sst, climatologyPeriod=[1993, 2022]).load()
    mhw = detect(sst, clim["thresh"], clim["seas"], minDuration=5,
                 joinGaps=True, maxGap=2)
```

### Which scheduler

We timed xmhw on the 20 × 20 block (400 ocean pixels) with each dask
scheduler, namely serial (`synchronous`), threads, the multiprocessing
scheduler (`processes`) and a `dask.distributed` `LocalCluster` with one
thread per worker process, from 1 to 8 workers (median of 2 runs).

```{r xmhw-scaling-fig, echo = FALSE, out.width = "85%", fig.alt = "Line chart of xmhw wall-clock time on 400 pixels against the number of dask workers, for the processes and distributed schedulers, with the serial time and ideal scaling as reference lines and the threaded scheduler at 8 workers as a single point."}
knitr::include_graphics("benchmark-data/xmhw_scaling_block.png")
```

```{r xmhw-scaling-table, echo = FALSE}
st <- sc[order(sc$variant, sc$threads), c("variant", "threads", "clim", "detect", "total")]
knitr::kable(st, digits = 1, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Scheduler", "Workers", "Climatology (s)",
                           "Detection (s)", "Total (s)"))
```

The threaded scheduler gains nothing (`r bsec(blk("threads", 8))` on 8
threads against `r bsec(blk("synchronous", 1))` serial). This is because the
per-cell work in xmhw is mostly Python and xarray overhead (the climatology
alone makes 366 small `quantile()` calls per cell), which holds Python's
global interpreter lock, so only one thread runs at a time. Worker processes
avoid the lock but have to receive each cell's data and computation from the
parent process. With `dask.distributed` this transfer costs more than the
work itself (`r bsec(blk("distributed", 1))` on one worker), and the time then
falls with more workers. The multiprocessing scheduler has less overhead and
is the fastest dask option, at `r bsec(blk("processes", 8))` on 8 workers, but
it gains little beyond 4 workers. This is consistent with the parent process,
which builds every cell's computation and assembles the results on a single
core, setting the pace, and with the M2's 4 efficiency cores being slower than
its 4 performance cores.

### Cost per cell grows with the domain

```{r per-cell, include = FALSE}
clim_cell_block <- sc$clim[sc$variant == "synchronous"] / 400
clim_cell_full  <- row(x1)$climatology_s / 5569
det_cell_full   <- row(x1)$detection_s / 5569
```

Serial xmhw takes `r sprintf("%.2f", clim_cell_block)` s per cell for the
climatology on the 400-cell block, but `r sprintf("%.2f", clim_cell_full)` s
per cell on the whole zone, whereas detection stays near
`r sprintf("%.3f", det_cell_full)` s per cell. This is consistent with
`threshold()` running a single `dask.compute()` over the computations of all
cells, which the parent process prepares and optimises on one core before any
worker starts, and whose cost grows faster than the number of cells. It also
explains why the dask schedulers gain less on the whole zone than on the
block: with 8 workers, the multiprocessing scheduler is
`r sprintf("%.1f", blk("synchronous", 1) / blk("processes", 8))` times faster
than serial on the block and `r sprintf("%.1f", s(x1) / s(xp8))` times faster
on the whole zone.

### Upper bound: independent processes

To see how fast xmhw could be on 8 cores without dask overhead, we also split
the zone into 8 latitude strips with about the same number of ocean pixels and
ran 8 serial xmhw processes at the same time, one per strip. This gives
`r secs(s(xt8))` for the whole zone (from the start of the first process to
the end of the last), against `r secs(s(x1))` serial, `r secs(s(xp8))` with
the multiprocessing scheduler and `r secs(s(xd8))` with `dask.distributed`.
It leaves the output as 8 separate files, which then have to be combined,
and the 8 processes together used `r sprintf("%.1f", row(xt8)$peak_ram_gb)` GB
of memory at their peak, nearly all of the 16 GB of the test machine.

## Agreement of the detected events

On the 20 × 20 block, each package's events are paired with heatwave3's on
pixel, start date and end date, and the paired metrics compared (intensities
at 4 decimals, as heatwave3 and heatwaveR round them).

```{r agreement, echo = FALSE}
# per-day differences of the cumulative intensity (|difference| / duration), 1 significant digit
per_day <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "fg", digits = 1)
ta <- agr[, 1:10]
ta$cum_day_median <- per_day(agr$intensity_cumulative_per_day_median_abs_diff)
ta$cum_day_max <- per_day(agr$intensity_cumulative_per_day_max_abs_diff)
ta <- ta[, c(1:9, 11, 12, 10)]
knitr::kable(ta, digits = 2, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
             align = c("l", rep("r", 11)),
             col.names = c("Package", "Events", "Events (heatwave3)",
                           "Paired (same dates)", "Peak date (%)",
                           "Duration (%)", "Mean intensity (%)",
                           "Max intensity (%)", "Cumulative intensity (%)",
                           "Cum. per day, median diff. (°C)",
                           "Cum. per day, max diff. (°C)", "Category (%)"))
```

The two columns after the cumulative intensity give its difference per
event day, namely the absolute difference of each paired event's cumulative
intensity divided by its duration, so that differences of long and short
events can be compared on the same scale.

```{r agreement-numbers, include = FALSE}
a <- function(p, k) agr[agr$package == p, k]
unpaired_pct <- function(p) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (1 - a(p, "paired_identical_dates") / a(p, "events")))
dT <- function(p, k) formatC(a(p, k), format = "fg", digits = 1)
```

heatwaveR and heatwave3 detect the same `r format(a("heatwaveR", "events"), big.mark = ",")`
events, and every event has an exact partner. The cumulative intensities that
differ at the fourth decimal come from the CSV file, which holds the
temperatures to 6 decimals; given the float32 values of the NetCDF file,
heatwaveR agrees with heatwave3 on every cumulative intensity. The two
categories that differ belong to events whose peak lies within rounding of a
class boundary, because `detect_event(categories = TRUE)` rounds the
temperatures to 4 decimals before it assigns the category, whereas heatwave3,
like `heatwaveR::category()`, uses the temperatures as read. marineHeatWaves
and xmhw each compute their own climatology, so their thresholds differ
slightly from heatwave3's. This means that
`r unpaired_pct("marineHeatWaves")` (marineHeatWaves) and
`r unpaired_pct("xmhw")` (xmhw) of their events start or end on a different
day, and that paired mean intensities differ by a median of
`r dT("marineHeatWaves", "intensity_mean_median_abs_diff")` °C and
`r dT("xmhw", "intensity_mean_median_abs_diff")` °C respectively (at most
`r dT("marineHeatWaves", "intensity_mean_max_abs_diff")` °C and
`r dT("xmhw", "intensity_mean_max_abs_diff")` °C). These differences are
concentrated in two periods of the year, namely around 29 February, which
each package handles in its own way, and, for marineHeatWaves only, around the
new year, where its window for the last days of the climatology period takes
data from the following January. Durations agree in every pair. Across the
whole zone, xmhw finds
`r format(cmp$full_zone_counts$events, big.mark = ",")` events against
heatwave3's `r format(cmp$full_zone_counts$events_heatwave3, big.mark = ",")`,
with the same count in `r cmp$full_zone_counts$pixels_same_count_pct`% of
pixels.

## Caveats

- One machine and one region. The ratios depend on the CPU (the M2 mixes
  performance and efficiency cores), the disk and the grid size.
- The heatwaveR and marineHeatWaves times are projections that exclude
  reading the data, which favours them.
- xmhw on the whole zone is a single run per configuration. On the 400-pixel
  block, the two runs of each configuration agreed to within 5%. In an
  earlier session, three `dask.distributed` runs on the block were up to 3
  times slower than these, for reasons we did not identify; they are not
  included.
- heatwave3 writes a CF-compliant event table and gridded climatology,
  whereas xmhw writes its climatology and an event array padded to the largest number of
  events in any cell. The output formats differ, but both are written to
  NetCDF within the timed run.

## Reproducing the benchmark

The calls below are the ones timed (heatwave3 shown in R; the Python package
takes the same arguments).

```{r hw3-call, eval = FALSE}
library(heatwave3)
sst_file <- "biscay_glorys12_full_1993-2025.nc"
ts2clm3(sst_file, name = "biscay", climatologyPeriod = c("1993-01-01", "2022-12-31"),
        var_name = "thetao", n_threads = 8)
detect_event3(sst_file, name = "biscay", var_name = "thetao", minDuration = 5,
              maxGap = 2, category = TRUE, hemisphere = "north", n_threads = 8)
```

```{r heatwaveR-call, eval = FALSE}
# heatwaveR, per pixel (ts: data.frame with t and temp)
clm <- heatwaveR::ts2clm(ts, climatologyPeriod = c("1993-01-01", "2022-12-31"))
ev  <- heatwaveR::detect_event(clm, categories = TRUE, S = FALSE)
```

```python
# marineHeatWaves, per pixel (t: ordinal days, sst: numpy array)
import marineHeatWaves as mhw
events, clim = mhw.detect(t, sst, climatologyPeriod=[1993, 2022],
                          minDuration=5, joinAcrossGaps=True, maxGap=2)
```

The xmhw call is shown above. The result files behind every table and figure
are in
[`vignettes/articles/benchmark-data/`](https://github.com/robwschlegel/heatwave3/tree/main/vignettes/articles/benchmark-data).
